title: The Śabarī on the High Mountain
summary: A Śabarī girl lives on a high mountain, dressed in peacock feathers with a guñjā garland at her neck, and roams the budding forest alone; the mad Śabara, told that his own wife is Innate Beauty, spreads a bed of the three worlds and passes the night in love with Nairātmā, the listener is told to pierce supreme nirvāṇa with the arrow of his own mind from the bow of the guru's word, and the mad Śabara enters a cleft in the mountain's peak. Munidatta reads the mountain as the yogin's body with Sumeru's peak and the Śabarī as Nairātmā, the wisdom seal (cp.28.m2, cp.28.m4), and the mad Śabara as the poet's own mind-vajra, drunk on the innate (cp.28.m8).

flags.note: The heading line names only the rāga. The poet's name comes from the attribution śabarapādānām, 'of Śabarapāda', which the manuscript writes before the song (removed from 1a as not part of the verse). The Tibetan heading names Saraha instead (sa ra ha'i zhabs kyi'o). I have kept the Nepal manuscript's attribution; see the witness note on the heading.

lines.translit: um̐cā um̐cā pābata tam̐him̐ basai sabarī bālī
lines.gloss: high · high · mountain · there · lives · Śabarī · girl
lines.en: On a high, high [mountain]{mountain}, there lives a [Śabarī]{sabari} girl.

lines.translit: moraṅgi pīccha parahiṇa sabarī gibata guñjarī mālī || dhru ||
lines.gloss: peacock's · feathers · garment · Śabarī · at the neck · guñjā-berry · garland · (cue to sing the refrain)
lines.en: In [peacock feathers]{peacock-feather} the [Śabarī]{sabari} is dressed, at her [neck]{kantha} a [guñjā garland]{gunja-garland}.

flags.note: গুঞ্জরী here is guñjā, the seed of the rosary-pea vine, strung as a garland (mālī). It is spelled like the rāga Guñjarī of song 5 but is a different word. The Tibetan has ma ru'i phreng ba, and its commentary glosses ma ru as guny+dza (cp.28.m2).

Shastri prints ধ্রু after this couplet, as after every later one: here it closes the refrain itself, which opens the song. Munidatta's remark at the end of his comment on couplet 1 marks the refrain here too; see the note on couplet 1. The cue is not translated.

lines.translit: umata sabaro pāgala śabaro mā kara gulī guhāḍā tohauri
lines.gloss: mad · Śabara · crazy · Śabara · do not · make · gulī (?) · guhāḍā (?) · your (?)

flags.note: gulī guhāḍā is not understood. Munidatta explains only 'do not make gulī', as 'do not form conceptual thoughts such as joy' (cp.28.m3); the Tibetan keeps gu li untranslated and has nothing for guhāḍā. Both words are kept in source form; guhāḍā is proposed as an entry (guhada) so that it is glossed.

tohauri, apparently 'your', is rendered where it stands. The Tibetan construes it with the next line: its 2b opens khyod kyi rang gi khyim mi mo, 'your own woman of the house', and its 2a ends with a second vocative sa wa ri instead.

umata (Sanskrit unmatta) is rendered 'mad' (unmatta), not 'drunk' (matta): the Tibetan has smyon pa, 'madman', and the line pairs it with pāgala, 'crazy'. pāgala is left unmarked as 'crazy', since the unmatta entry lists the form but has no variant 'crazy'.

lines.translit: ṇia ghariṇī ṇāme sahaja sundārī || dhru ||
lines.gloss: own · wife · by name · innate · beauty · (cue to sing the refrain)

flags.note: 'your' is what English needs with ṇia, 'own', in an address; if tohauri (2a) belongs to this line, as the Tibetan takes it, the English is unchanged.

lines.translit: ṇāṇā tarubara maulilare gaaṇata lāgelī ḍālī
lines.gloss: various · fine trees · budded (?) · in the sky · touched · branches
lines.en: The various [fine trees]{taruvara} have come into bud; their [branches]{branch} touch the [sky]{gagana}.

flags.note: maulilare: 'have come into bud' follows Munidatta's mukulita, 'budded' (cp.28.m4). The Tibetan line has rtse mo, 'tops' ('the tops of the various fine trees'), as if from mauli, 'crown, top'. The ending -re is unexplained, perhaps an emphatic particle.

lines.translit: ekelī sabarī e baṇa hiṇḍai karṇakuṇḍalabajradhārī || dhru ||
lines.gloss: alone · Śabarī · this · forest · roams · bearing ear-rings and vajra · (cue to sing the refrain)
lines.en: Alone, the [Śabarī]{sabari} roams this [forest]{forest}, bearing [earrings]{kundala} and a [vajra]{vajra}.

flags.note: The Tibetan line lists three things, rna rgyan 'khor lo rdo rje 'dzin, 'earrings, wheel, holding a vajra', adding a wheel the Bengali lacks. rdo rje 'dzin is also the usual name of Vajradhara, but here it renders bajradhārī, 'bearing a vajra'.
The compound could be read 'bearing vajra earrings'; Munidatta (cp.28.m4) and the Tibetan both take the earrings and the vajra as two things.

lines.translit: tia dhāu khāṭa paṛilā sabaro mahāsukhe seji chāilī
lines.gloss: three · worlds (realms) · bed · was laid · Śabara · with great bliss · bedding · spread
lines.en: The [bed]{bed} of the [three worlds]{trailokya} was laid; the [Śabara]{sabara} spread the [bedding]{bed} with [great bliss]{mahasukha}.

flags.note: paṛilā is read as intransitive, 'was laid' (compare Munidatta's ṭālayitvā and the Tibetan brkyang nas, 'spread out', cp.28.m5), with the Śabara as the one who spreads the bedding. It can also be read 'the Śabara laid a bed of the three worlds'. The Tibetan line names no Śabara here.

lines.translit: sabaro bhujaṅga ṇairāmaṇi dārī pehma rāti pohāilī || dhru ||
lines.gloss: Śabara · lover (snake?) · Nairātmā · courtesan (wife? girl?) · in love · night · brought to dawn · (cue to sing the refrain)
lines.en: The [Śabara]{sabara} a [lover]{bhujanga}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma} a [courtesan]{dari}: in [love]{prema} they passed the [night]{rajani} till dawn.

flags.note: bhujaṅga: literally 'snake'; in Sanskrit poetry also a lover, gallant or rake, the sense its pairing with dārī suggests. The Tibetan takes it as 'snake' (sbrul in the line, ltos 'gro, 'belly-crawler', in the comment); Munidatta equates it with the Śabara's mind-vajra (cp.28.m5) without showing which sense he hears. I used the glossary's 'lover'.

dārī: 'courtesan' follows the glossary and the Tibetan (gzugs 'tshong ma). Sanskrit dārāḥ is 'wife', which would answer 'your own wife' in 2b, and dārikā is 'girl'. Munidatta's derivation from dārayati, 'she tears apart (the afflictions)' (cp.28.m5), is an etymology, not a sense.
The song writes ṇairāmaṇi here and nirāmaṇi in 5b; I used the glossary's English, Nairātmā.

lines.gloss: heart · betel · in great bliss · camphor · eats
lines.en: With the [heart]{hrdaya} for [betel]{betel}, in [great bliss]{mahasukha} he eats [camphor]{camphor}.

flags.note: The Tibetan line has sems, 'mind', for hia, 'heart'; the Tibetan commentary has snying, 'heart' (cp.28.m6).
khāi, 'eats', has no stated subject; 'he' (the Śabara) is supplied for English.

lines.translit: suna nirāmaṇi kaṇṭhe laiā mahāsuhe rāti pohāi || dhru ||
lines.gloss: empty (emptiness) · Nairātmā · at the neck · having taken · in great bliss · night · brings to dawn · (cue to sing the refrain)
lines.en: Taking [emptiness]{sunyata}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, at his [neck]{kantha}, in [great bliss]{mahasukha} he passes the [night]{rajani} till dawn.

flags.note: suna (śūnya) qualifies Nirāmaṇi: 'empty Nirāmaṇi'. To keep the glossary's English, 'emptiness', I set it in apposition ('emptiness, Nairātmā'), which agrees with Munidatta's 'she is emptiness' (cp.28.m6); 'empty Nairātmā' would be closer to the Bengali.
The Tibetan line makes Nairātmā the subject, bdag med ma yis mgul nas 'khyud, 'Nairātmā embraces (him) at the neck', where the Bengali has him take her at the neck.

lines.translit: gurubāka puñcaā bindha ṇia maṇe bāṇem̐
lines.gloss: guru's word · bow · pierce · own · with mind · with arrow
lines.en: With the [guru]{guru}'s word for a [bow]{bow}, pierce with your own [mind]{citta} for an [arrow]{arrow}.

flags.note: puñcaā is rendered 'bow' on the evidence of Munidatta's dhanus (cp.28.m7) and the Tibetan gzhu; I cannot derive the Old Bengali word.

lines.translit: eke śarasandhānem̐ bindhaha bindhaha parama ṇibāṇem̐ || dhru ||
lines.gloss: with one · with fitting of the arrow · pierce · pierce · supreme · nirvāṇa (at, into) · (cue to sing the refrain)
lines.en: With the [arrow]{arrow} fitted once, pierce, pierce supreme [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}!

flags.note: ṇibāṇem̐ has the -em̐ ending (instrumental or locative), so 'pierce into supreme nirvāṇa' is also possible; the Tibetan makes nirvāṇa the thing pierced (mchog gi mya ngan 'das pa phug).

The poet names himself here (the bhaṇitā). সবরো is tagged sabara, not p-sabara: umata sabaro repeats the opening words of 2a, the approved English of p-sabara is 'Śabarapāda', which the song does not say, and Munidatta reads this Śabara as 'my mind-vajra' (cp.28.m8). See the note on the bhaṇitā and the questions.

lines.translit: giribara sihara sandhi paisante sabaro loṛiba kaise || dhru ||
lines.gloss: finest of mountains · peak · cleft · on entering · Śabara · is to be sought (will seek?) · how · (cue to sing the refrain)
lines.en: entering the cleft of the great [mountain]{mountain}'s peak, how is the [Śabara]{sabara} to be sought?

flags.note: loṛiba is read as a gerundive, 'is to be sought', with the Śabara as the one sought. Both witnesses make him the seeker: Munidatta has 'how is the meaning I stated to be sought by me, the siddha master?' (cp.28.m8), and the Tibetan line 'how shall I leap?' (bdag gis ji ltar mchong bar byed). The alternative English is 'how will the Śabara search?'.
The Tibetan line has mchong, 'leap', where its commentary, like the Sanskrit, has 'seek' (btsal; anveṣayitavya).

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music; the heading names the melody to which the song is sung. Shastri's balāḍḍi is the glossary's Varāḍī, the rāga of song 21. The Tibetan heading transcribes it bar Di and calls it a glu dbyangs, 'melody'.

Attribution. The Nepal manuscript writes śabarapādānām, 'of Śabarapāda', before the song (Shastri prints it at the head of 1a; it is removed from the verse). Munidatta names the poet [Śabarapāda]{p-sabara} at the opening of his comment (cp.28.m1) and makes him speak at couplet 6: mayā savarapādena, 'by me, Śabarapāda' (cp.28.m7). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) divides. Its heading names [Saraha]{p-saraha} (/bar Di zhes pa'i glu dbyangs sa ra ha'i zhabs kyi'o/, 'the melody called Bar Ḍi, of Sarahapāda'), and at cp.28.m7 it has sa ra ha'i zhabs bdag gis, 'by me, Sarahapāda', where the Sanskrit has Śabarapāda. But at cp.28.m1 it agrees with the Sanskrit (grub pa'i slob dpon sa wa ri pa'i zhabs), and its line of the bhaṇitā calls the poet sha wa ri pa (7a). Both versions of the comment on couplet 4 quote Saraha by name as another author (cp.28.m5). The attribution to Śabarapāda is kept; the Tibetan's Saraha is recorded here for the reviewer.

Śabarī: a woman of the Śabaras, a forest and hill people of eastern and central India whom caste society treated as outsiders. bālī is 'girl, young woman'; the Tibetan has sa wa ri yi bu mo, 'the Śabara girl' (bu mo, 'girl, daughter'). The doubled um̐cā, 'high, high', is kept as the song has it.

Munidatta reads the high mountain as the raised staff of the skeleton of the lord of yogis' own body (the Tibetan: the rod of the spine, sgal tshigs kyi dbyig pa), at the tip of Sumeru's peak, in the wheel of great bliss. Where the song has 'there lives a Śabarī girl', he has 'his wife, the jñānamudrā Nairātmā, born of the syllable aṃ, dwells' (the Tibetan: born of a). 'His' is the vajra-holder (pavidhara), introduced by a play on letters, 'the ha that follows sa', which the Tibetan renders 'the one who holds that ha beyond the syllable sa is the Śabara' (sa wa ri); how the letters yield the name is not explained (cp.28.m2).

Guñjā berries are the glossy red, black-spotted seeds of the rosary-pea vine, strung as necklaces; with the peacock feathers they make the dress of a forest woman. gibata is 'at the neck' (Sanskrit grīvā, as in Munidatta's grīvāyām, cp.28.m2). parahiṇa (Sanskrit paridhāna) is 'garment'. The Tibetan line has the plumes 'worn on the body' (lus la gyon) and the garland 'hung at the neck' (mgul du dpyangs).

Munidatta glosses the peacock feathers (mayūrāṅga, 'peacock limb') as the many varied forms of conceptual thought about sides (pakṣa, also 'wing, feather'), made into her garment and ornament as they rest in their own nature; and the guñjā garland as the secret mantra (guhyamantra) held at the neck, the wheel of enjoyment (sambhogacakra). The Sanskrit of that clause is partly corrupt (āvike 'pi); the Tibetan has 'the secret mantra of guhya' and glosses the line's ma ru as guñjā (guny+dza) (cp.28.m2).

The [refrain]{dhruvapada}. In this song the refrain is the opening couplet, not the second. Munidatta ends his comment on couplet 1 with padasyottarapadena dhruvapadaṃ boddhavyam, 'by the latter line of the verse the refrain is to be understood', that is, by 1b (cp.28.m2); the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) says the same (rkang pa gzhan gyi rkang pas d+hU'i rkang par shes par bya'o). Shastri's ধ্রু after 1b agrees. Taken strictly, the remark names the second line; the whole couplet is marked as the refrain, as refrains elsewhere in the songs are whole couplets. Because the refrain opens the song, his count starts from it: couplet 2 is his 'second verse', which states the nature of practice (dvitīyapadena abhyāsasvarūpam āha, cp.28.m3; the Tibetan rkang pa gnyis pas goms pa'i rang bzhin gsungs so); his comment on couplet 3 carries no number (cp.28.m4); and couplets 4 to 7 are his third to sixth verses (cp.28.m5 to cp.28.m8). So in this song it is couplet 3, not the refrain, that his count passes over.

Śabara: a man of the Śabaras, the forest and hill people of the Śabarī. In couplet 2 he is addressed; in couplet 4 he is the Śabarī's lover; in the last couplet the poet takes the name himself. The Tibetan transcribes the word sa wa ri, as for the woman.

gulī and guhāḍā are kept in source form. The meaning of gulī is unknown: the Tibetan keeps it as gu li, and Munidatta explains 'do not make gulī' as 'do not form conceptual thoughts such as joy' (cp.28.m3), a reading rather than a sense. Neither witness explains guhāḍā. tohauri is taken as 'your'.

umata is Sanskrit unmatta, 'mad, out of one's mind', and pāgala is 'crazy'. The Tibetan has smyon pa, 'madman', here and in 7a. Munidatta first takes it as 'mad', addressing the Śabara as one whose mind is overwhelmed by sense objects (viṣayavihvalacitta, cp.28.m3); at the bhaṇitā he glosses it 'intoxicated with drinking the innate' (sahajapānapramatta, cp.28.m8). 'Mad' renders the word; 'drunk' is his reading at 7a.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of couplet 2 reads /smyon pa sa wa ri ni 'khrul/ /gu li ma byed sa wa ri/ /khyod kyi rang gi khyim mi mo/ /ming ni lhan skyes mdzes ldan ma/: 'the mad Śabara is deluded; do not make gu li, Śabara; your own woman of the house is named Innate Beauty'. It has nothing for guhāḍā, adds 'khrul, 'deluded' (perhaps for pāgala), and takes 'your' with the wife.

Munidatta introduces couplet 2 as his second verse, stating the nature of practice, and puts it in the mouth of the Blessed Lady Nairātmā, who comforts the Śabara in the union of wisdom and means: 'O mad Śabara, whose mind is overwhelmed by sense objects, do not form conceptual thoughts such as joy; I am your wife, the jñānamudrā, Sahajasundarī' (cp.28.m3). The song does not name the speaker.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads couplet 3 /sna tshogs shing mchog rtse mo ni/ /nam mkha'i mthil du yal ga reg/ /gcig pur sa wa ri nyid 'gro/ /rna rgyan 'khor lo rdo rje 'dzin/: 'the tops of the various fine trees touch the depth of the sky with their branches; the Śabarī goes alone, holding earrings, wheel and vajra'. It has 'tops' (rtse mo) where Munidatta has 'budded' (mukulita) for maulilare, and adds a wheel ('khor lo). Its comment likewise begins the five seals, which it calls bone ornaments (rus pa'i rgyan), with the wheel, where the Sanskrit begins with the earrings (kuṇḍalādi) (cp.28.m4).

vajra: the ritual sceptre of tantric Buddhism, 'thunderbolt' and 'diamond', carried by its deities and adepts. karṇakuṇḍalabajradhārī is 'bearing earrings and vajra'; hiṇḍai is 'roams, wanders about'.

Munidatta places the couplet on 'this body-Sumeru'. The fine tree has the form of ignorance and, by the mantra of joy and the rest, has come in various ways into its own budded form; its branches are the five aggregates, touching the sky, which he calls clear light. 'Therefore that Nairātmā is alone' stands where the song has 'alone, the Śabarī'. The earrings head the five seals (pañcamudrā), worn as ornament, apparently with no garment (niraṃśuka); the vajra is the knowledge of means, held in the form of coupled union, 'here in the forest of the body-mountain'; and 'roams' (hiṇḍati) means 'plays' (krīḍati) (cp.28.m4).

khāṭa is a cot or bedstead (Sanskrit khaṭvā), seji (Sanskrit śayyā) the bedding spread on it; chāilī, 'spread, covered'. tia dhāu (Sanskrit traidhātuka) is 'the three realms'; the glossary renders it 'three worlds'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of 4a names no Śabara (/khams gsum po yi khri nyid bshams/ /bde ba chen po'i nyal sa byas/, 'the bed of the three worlds was set out; the sleeping place of great bliss was made'). In 4b it reads bhujaṅga as 'snake' (/sa wa ri sbrul bdag med ma/ /gzugs 'tshong dga' bas nam langs gyur/, 'the Śabara a snake, Nairātmā a courtesan; with joy the dawn came'), and keeps that sense in its comment, ltos 'gro, 'belly-crawler' (cp.28.m5).

bhujaṅga is literally 'snake' (the one that moves in coils); in Sanskrit poetry it also means a lover, gallant or rake, often a courtesan's lover. Beside dārī, which the Tibetan renders gzugs 'tshong ma, 'courtesan' (literally 'seller of the body'), that second sense fits, and the couplet pairs a lover and a courtesan. Munidatta's text has bhuja(ca)ṅga, the edition marking a doubtful letter, and his gloss, 'the Śabara's mind-vajra', does not show which sense he hears (cp.28.m5).

Nairātmā, 'she who is without self': selflessness personified as a goddess in the Hevajra tradition. The song writes ṇairāmaṇi here and nirāmaṇi in 5b, Old Bengali forms of the name; Munidatta writes nairātmā (cp.28.m5, cp.28.m6), and the Tibetan bdag med ma. pehma is Sanskrit prema, 'love' (the Tibetan: dga' bas, 'with joy'); pohāilī, 'brought (the night) to dawn', is the verb for a night that ends.

Munidatta introduces couplet 4 as 'the flow of the bliss of play' (krīḍāsukhapravāha; the Tibetan has 'strength', stobs). The three worlds are body, speech and mind, spread out (the Tibetan: stretched, brkyang) in the clear light of bliss; with that great bliss a bed is made, together with the bhujaṅga, the Śabara's mind-vajra. Nairātmā is the dārikā 'because she tears apart (dārayati) the afflictions'; love (prema) is the incomparable flavour of play, made to grow; and the night is the darkness, the conceptual thought of wisdom and means, destroyed. He closes with a line of Saraha, 'Śrī Vajrāmṛta…' (cp.28.m5).

Betel: a quid of areca nut and lime wrapped in a betel leaf, flavoured with spices such as camphor, chewed for pleasure and shared by lovers. Here the heart is the betel, and camphor is eaten with it.

Munidatta introduces couplet 5 as setting out the power that is the relation of fruit and cause. The heart is clear light, resolved upon (adhimucya) as the betel; camphor is coupled union, resolved upon through that relation. 'Empty' is Nairātmā herself, 'emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects', the yoginī of the knowledge of selflessness; 'at the neck' is held at the wheel of enjoyment; and 'night' is the darkness of the afflictions of one's own body, destroyed of itself by the ray of the knowledge of great bliss. He cites the Sūtaka: 'having sealed the cause with the fruit…' (cp.28.m6).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of couplet 5 reads /sems ni so rtsi bde ba che/ /ga bur za ba stong pa yi/ /bdag med ma yis mgul nas 'khyud/ /bde chen mtshan mo nam langs gyur/: 'the mind is betel, great bliss; eating camphor, the empty Nairātmā embraces (him) at the neck; the night of great bliss turns to dawn'. It has 'mind' for 'heart', moves 'empty' (stong pa yi) into its second line, and makes Nairātmā the one who embraces. Its comment on the couplet opens with the wrong lemma, rma bya'i mdongs, 'peacock plumes' (the opening of 1b), where the Sanskrit has hiem̐ ityādi, and calls the betel go la (cp.28.m6).

puñcaā: I cannot derive the Old Bengali word for the bow; 'bow' rests on Munidatta's dhanus (cp.28.m7) and the Tibetan gzhu. gurubāka is guru-vākya, 'the guru's word'. śarasandhāna (6b) is the fitting of the arrow to the string, taking aim; the Tibetan has mda' gcig nyid ni bsdogs byas nas, 'having fitted a single arrow'.

Munidatta introduces couplet 6 as the greatness of the vajra guru. The true guru's word is made the bow and one's own mind, bodhicitta, the arrow; the single arrow is 'the arrow of one taste' (ekarasa), the two made one. Practising it with the resounding of a single sound (ekasvaranirghoṣa), he says, 'by that nirvāṇa, by me, Śabarapāda, the fault of the habitual tendencies of beginningless ignorance has been slain' (cp.28.m7). He opened the whole comment by calling Śabarapāda 'pierced by the flavour of great compassion' (cp.28.m1).

The bhaṇitā. The poet signs the song by naming the mad Śabara of couplet 2: umata sabaro in 7a repeats the opening words of 2a, so poet and figure meet. I have tagged সবরো in 7a and 7b as sabara (Śabara), as in 2a, 4a and 4b, rather than p-sabara: the approved English of p-sabara is Śabarapāda, with the honorific -pāda the song never uses; tagging the echo differently from 2a would split one phrase between two entries; and Munidatta reads the Śabara of 7a as the poet's mind-vajra, not the man (cp.28.m8). The case for p-sabara is strongest in 7b, where Munidatta speaks as 'me, the siddha master' and the Tibetan has bdag gis, 'by me'. The poet himself is linked in the heading.

giribara is 'finest of mountains', sihara (śikhara) 'peak', sandhi 'joint, cleft, juncture': the Śabara enters a cleft in the summit. loṛiba is read as a gerundive of loṛ-, 'seek', as Munidatta's anveṣayitavya suggests (cp.28.m8).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) renders the last couplet /smyon pa sha wa ri pa ni/ /cher khros ri bo mchog rtse yi/ /mtshams su zhugs nas sha wa ri/ /bdag gis ji ltar mchong bar byed/: 'the madman Śavaripa, greatly enraged, having entered the cleft of the best mountain's peak, Śavari: how shall I leap?'. It names the poet with the suffix -pa (sha wa ri pa), as its comment does at the opening (cp.28.m1), puts the verb in the first person (bdag gis), and has mchong, 'leap', where its own comment, like Munidatta's Sanskrit, has 'seek' (btsal; anveṣayitavya) (cp.28.m8).

Munidatta introduces the last couplet as stating the mind's true nature as it is. The mad Śabara is 'my mind-vajra, intoxicated with drinking the innate'; 'in great rage' means impelled by the scent of the joy of knowledge and set moving toward the lotus grove of the wheel of great bliss; when it has sunk there, 'how is the meaning I have stated to be sought by me, the siddha master?'. He quotes scripture: as long as the mind goes on there is no end of vehicles; when the mind has turned to reality there is neither vehicle nor traveller (cp.28.m8).

termsOmitted.reason: Tibetan heading only (sa ra ha'i zhabs); the Bengali names no Saraha, and the attribution to Śabarapāda is kept (see the witness note).
Tibetan only: rdo rje 'dzin renders bajradhārī, 'bearing a vajra', not the buddha Vajradhara.
Tibetan only: its line adds 'khor lo, a wheel the Bengali does not have.
Detected in the Tibetan (sha wa ri pa); the Bengali সবরো is tagged sabara for the reasons in the bhaṇitā note, pending the reviewer's decision.
False hit: the Tibetan sha is the first syllable of sha wa ri (Śabara), not 'flesh'.

proposals.definition: A bed: a cot or bedstead (Old Bengali khāṭa, from Sanskrit khaṭvā) and the bedding spread on it (seji, Sanskrit śayyā). In song 28 a bed of the three worlds is laid and its bedding spread with great bliss, where the Śabara and Nairātmā pass the night. The Tibetan has khri, 'seat, bed', and nyal sa, 'sleeping place'.
proposals.symbolicImage: a bed of the three worlds, its bedding spread with great bliss

symbolicReadings.referent: a bed made 'with that great bliss' once the three realms, body, speech and mind, have been spread out in the clear light of bliss, shared with the Śabara's mind-vajra; a paraphrase rather than an explicit gloss of the bed

proposals.rationale: The bed is a concrete image of song 28 that the commentary takes up (śayyā); the glossary has no entry for khāṭa or seji, and an entry lets the woven commentary and any later song link to it.

proposals.definition: A word of unknown sense in couplet 2 of song 28 (2a), paired with gulī: the mad Śabara is told not to make gulī guhāḍā. Munidatta explains only gulī (cp.28.m3), and the Tibetan line, which keeps gu li, has nothing for it. Kept in source form until its sense is found.
proposals.rationale: The draft keeps guhāḍā in source form in 2a; without an entry it would stand unglossed beside gulī, which has one.

proposals.definition: Love (Old Bengali pehma, Sanskrit preman), the love in which the Śabara and Nairātmā pass the night until dawn in song 28. The Tibetan line has dga' bas, 'with joy'. Munidatta glosses it as the incomparable flavour of play (krīḍārasa), made to grow (cp.28.m5).
proposals.symbolicImage: the love in which the lovers pass the night until dawn

symbolicReadings.referent: the incomparable flavour of play (krīḍārasa), which is made to grow; the Tibetan comment has 'the incomparable play increases' (rol pa'i dpe med pa 'phel bar 'gyur ro)

proposals.rationale: pehma is a plain word of the song with an explicit gloss in the commentary; an entry records that gloss and keeps 'play' out of the line.

proposals.definition: Rage, anger (Sanskrit roṣa). In the last couplet of song 28 the mad Śabara, in great rage (garuā roṣe), enters the cleft of the mountain's peak; the Tibetan has cher khros, 'greatly enraged'. Munidatta reads the rage as the impulse of the scent of the joy of knowledge (cp.28.m8).
proposals.symbolicImage: the mad Śabara's great rage as he enters the cleft of the peak

symbolicReadings.referent: being impelled by the scent of the joy of knowledge (jñānānandagandha) and set moving toward the lotus grove of the wheel of great bliss; the Tibetan comment agrees (ye shes kyi dga' ba'i dris bskul bar gyur pa)

proposals.rationale: The word carries an explicit, unexpected gloss in the commentary; an entry records it and keeps the reading out of the line.

questions: Self-naming (7a, 7b): I tagged সবরো as sabara, not p-sabara (reasons in the bhaṇitā note). If you want the signature linked to the poet, as in other bhaṇitās, p-sabara needs 'Śabara' as a variant, since its English, Śabarapāda, is not what the song says. Retag both lines, only 7b (where Munidatta and the Tibetan make the poet speak in the first person), or neither?

umata: I used unmatta, 'mad', not matta, 'drunk'. Please confirm, and consider moving the form unmatto out of the matta entry. May 'crazy' be added as a variant of unmatta, so that pāgala in 2a can be tagged too?
bhujaṅga (4b): I kept the glossary's 'lover' against the Tibetan 'snake' (sbrul). Would you prefer 'paramour' or 'gallant', or the literal 'snake'?
dārī (4b): 'courtesan' (glossary; Tibetan gzugs 'tshong ma), 'wife' (Sanskrit dārāḥ; compare 'your own wife' in 2b) or 'girl' (dārikā)?
puñcaā (6a): 'bow' rests only on Munidatta's dhanus and the Tibetan gzhu. Do you know a derivation, or should the bow entry say plainly that the Old Bengali word is unexplained?
suna (5b): the Bengali reads 'empty Nirāmaṇi'. To keep the glossary's 'emptiness' I put it in apposition ('emptiness, Nairātmā'). May 'empty' be added as a variant of sunyata for adjectival uses?
The song calls the goddess Ṇairāmaṇi (4b) and Nirāmaṇi (5b); I used the glossary's Nairātmā. Keep it, or add the song's form as a variant?

2a: gulī guhāḍā is unexplained and kept in source form (I propose an entry, guhada). Is tohauri 'your', and does it go with 2a, where it stands, or with 'your own wife' in 2b, as the Tibetan takes it?

7b: I read 'how is the Śabara to be sought?' (gerundive, the Śabara sought). Munidatta and the Tibetan make him the seeker ('how is it to be sought by me', 'how shall I leap'). Which reading do you want?
Heading: I added '· Śabarapāda' from the attribution written before the song (emended out of 1a), since the heading line names only the rāga. Is that how you want headings to carry the poet?
3a maulilare: 'have come into bud' (Munidatta's mukulita) or 'the tops of the trees' (the Tibetan rtse mo)?

Glossary: the existing entries grhini, guhada, guli, sahaja-sundari and unmatta describe couplet 2 as 'the refrain of song 28' (sahaja-sundari also has Munidatta put 'the refrain' in Nairātmā's mouth). With couplet 1 now marked as the refrain, they need 'couplet 2' instead. A proposal does not change an existing entry, so I could correct only my own proposal for guhada; please amend the five definitions.
